clue.text: 75% .absenteeism in the office.? Calls for a big stick

explanation.surface: A manager notes that three-quarters of the office has failed to turn up, and someone wants to bring out the cane.
explanation.walkthrough: With 75% of the office absent, only a quarter of the staff is left at work. 'Calls for' is the link to the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: If three in four workers are away, a fourth of the workforce remains; a quarterstaff is also a long wooden pole once used as a weapon.

clue.text: Naming a price — in inverted commas?

explanation.surface: A seller names a figure, but says it with an air of quotation marks.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who states a cost gives an estimate; words set inside quotation marks are being cited from someone else.

clue.text: Base is a number about 51

indicators.note: the number goes round the other piece, so 'about' signals one piece placed around another

parts.note: nine is a number
LI is 51 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A chemist mentions that a certain base has a number of about fifty-one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like a foundation, but it is the chemistry sense; the number goes round LI in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Aniline is an organic compound that acts as a chemical base, used for making dyes.

clue.text: The Council's officer seems safer after rate revision

indicators.note: the safer piece comes after the reworked rate piece in the answer
a revision rewrites something, so the letters of the word rate are reworked into a new order

parts.note: surer means safer, more certain

explanation.surface: A town hall finance official feels more secure once the local rates have been revised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seems' is a link word; rates were Britain's old local property tax, collected by the council.
explanation.definitionFit: A council's finance officer who looks after its funds holds that title.

clue.text: Where, out West, they ran both taps ?

parts.note: taken as written
C and H are the marks on the cold and hot taps

explanation.surface: Someone in the Wild West runs a bath with both taps going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they' is a link word; the two taps of a basin are marked C (cold) and H (hot).
explanation.definitionFit: A large cattle farm in the American West is the place meant.

clue.text: A buffoon more known than knowing

definitions.text: A buffoon more known than knowing

parts.words: A buffoon more known than knowing
parts.note: a clown who is well known (has a familiar name like Tom) but knows little: a silly person

explanation.surface: A clown is famous for being famous rather than for any wisdom.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'known' half suggests a familiar first name, the 'knowing' half that the fellow is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A silly, foolish person or clown is called by this old word.

clue.text: Getting' the wind up 'when things get hot ?

definitions.text: Getting' the wind up 'when things get hot ?

parts.words: Getting' the wind up 'when things get hot
parts.note: 'getting the wind up' normally means becoming frightened, but here it means stirring a breeze to cool down in hot weather

explanation.surface: Someone loses their nerve as soon as matters become heated.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'get the wind up' means to panic; read literally it is waving air around to cool off.
explanation.definitionFit: Waving a fan makes moving air, which cools a person in heat.

clue.text: This for the rubber, and wealth untold

definitions.text: This for the rubber, and wealth untold

parts.words: This for the rubber, and wealth untold
parts.note: in the tale, rubbing a magic lamp summons a genie who brings riches

explanation.surface: A card player hopes for a winning rubber and huge riches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubber' suggests bridge or an eraser, but here it is the person who rubs the lamp in the Arabian Nights story.
explanation.definitionFit: The magic lamp of the Arabian Nights tale, rubbed to call up a genie granting riches.

clue.text: Like the heavenly sign of certain Popes

explanation.surface: Something resembles a sign of the zodiac and belongs to several pontiffs.
explanation.walkthrough: The heavenly sign is Leo, the lion; several Popes were called Leo.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means lion-like, recalling Leo the zodiac sign, and also relates to Popes named Leo, as in the Leonine City of Rome.

clue.text: Like rents without tears

parts.note: a rent so small that paying it causes no grief, a token sum

explanation.surface: Rents paid without tears, or garments without rips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rents' and 'tears' both suggest rips in cloth, but the rents are payments small enough not to cause weeping.
explanation.definitionFit: A token rent is set at a trivial sum, in name only.

clue.text: With no centre of gravity?

parts.note: the centre of a person is the heart, and having no gravity there means a weightless, carefree heart

explanation.surface: A physics puzzle about an object lacking a balance point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of gravity' looks like physics, but 'centre' is the heart and 'gravity' is seriousness or weight.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheerful, carefree person has a heart free of heaviness or solemnity.

clue.text: The papers say David is a liar

parts.note: Dai is a Welsh pet form of David
lies means tells untruths, as a liar does

explanation.surface: Someone claims the press says David is dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' is a link word introducing the example; Dai is the usual Welsh short form of David.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers published every day are called by this plural noun.

clue.text: Catching a pirate in Guatemala's capital

parts.note: Captain Hook is the pirate in Peter Pan

indicators.note: a capital letter is the first one, so the opening letter of the country is taken

explanation.surface: Someone captures a buccaneer in Guatemala City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' suggests the city, but it means the capital letter G.
explanation.definitionFit: Catching a fish on a barbed metal hook is this; seizing in general.

clue.text: Cosy nook in Wardle's Dell

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the name, with its outer letters dropped away

parts.note: Dingley Dell is Mr Wardle's home in Dickens's Pickwick Papers

explanation.surface: A snug corner is found at a country home from a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are held within DINGLEY, the first word of Dingley Dell, Mr Wardle's manor in Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: An inglenook is a chimney corner by the fire, a snug seat.

clue.text: The earl, though all-round Conservative, is a red on the road

indicators.note: the political word goes all round the nobleman, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: the right is the Conservative side of politics
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Tory nobleman is surprisingly described as a red on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red' looks like a socialist set against Conservative, but it is a red lamp on a car; 'though' and 'is' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: The red lamp at the back of a vehicle is seen by drivers behind it.

clue.text: Carrying off about 600 in confusion

indicators.note: in confusion the letters of the words are thrown into disorder

parts.note: DC is 600 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Something is carried away amid confusion, roughly six hundred of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram pool is ABOUT, DC and IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidnapping is the act of taking someone away by force.

clue.text: Sporadic car tested and repaired

indicators.note: a repaired car is put back together, so the letters of the words are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A car has been tested and mended only now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link word; the anagram is of CAR TESTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Things occurring here and there, at irregular intervals, are spread out.

clue.text: After five Miss Oakley reorganized its capital

definitions.text: After five Miss Oakley reorganized its capital

parts.words: After five Miss Oakley reorganized its capital
parts.note: V (five) followed by ANNIE (Annie Oakley) rearranged gives VIENNA, and the answer is the country whose capital that is

explanation.surface: After five o'clock, Annie Oakley reorganises the capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds the capital, VIENNA, not the answer; the solver then names the country that has it. Annie Oakley was a famous American sharpshooter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vienna is the capital city of this central European country.

clue.text: Touching an angel of France in explosive surroundings

indicators.note: the explosive forms the surroundings, so the other piece is placed inside it

parts.note: TNT is a high explosive
ange is French for an angel

explanation.surface: A French angel caught amid explosions is a moving sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link word; T-ANGE-NT.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a line meeting a curve at one point just touches it.

clue.text: Macavity, like Moriarty, was its Napoleon

definitions.text: Macavity, like Moriarty, was its Napoleon

parts.words: Macavity, like Moriarty, was its Napoleon
parts.note: both T. S. Eliot's cat Macavity and Holmes's foe Moriarty are called the Napoleon of lawbreaking

explanation.surface: Two famous villains are compared with a French emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: Holmes calls Moriarty 'the Napoleon of crime', and Eliot borrows the phrase for Macavity the Mystery Cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawbreaking as a whole is the field in which both villains were masterminds.

clue.text: A vulgar tune sounds the main danger

indicators.note: sounds says the words are judged by how they are spoken

parts.note: a coarse air is a vulgar tune

explanation.surface: A crude melody is said to be the chief threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' looks like 'chief', but it is the sea: a pirate is a danger on the main.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirate ship or its captain menaced shipping on the high seas.

clue.text: Elementary ? It could be at the, tip of your pen

definitions.text: Elementary ? It could be at the, tip of your pen

parts.words: Elementary ? It could be at the, tip of your pen
parts.note: a chemical element, a hard metal used to tip fountain-pen nibs

explanation.surface: A simple matter, perhaps, found at the end of a pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elementary' suggests 'simple' but means 'a chemical element'.
explanation.definitionFit: This very hard metallic element is used on the tips of pen nibs.

clue.text: Shoot ! This side has the necessary material

definitions.text: Shoot ! This side has the necessary material

parts.words: Shoot ! This side has the necessary material
parts.note: a football side whose players shoot, and also a store of weapons for shooting

explanation.surface: A football crowd urges a team with good players to shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal is a London football club; the 'material' is the weaponry stored in an armoury.
explanation.definitionFit: A store of weapons and ammunition; also the name of a London football club.

clue.text: Alert for' change in the future

indicators.note: a change of arrangement means the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone stays watchful for coming changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: At a subsequent time, afterwards, is this adverb's sense.

clue.text: Not that this pigeon infects others

definitions.text: Not that this pigeon infects others

parts.words: Not that this pigeon infects others
parts.note: a homing pigeon of one kind, though the word also means a person who passes on disease

explanation.surface: A bird fancier reassures everyone that the pigeon is not contagious.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is a carrier pigeon; a disease carrier infects others.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigeon trained to bear messages; also one who transmits infection.

clue.text: Tense from much practice ?

explanation.surface: Someone gets nervous after rehearsing a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like 'anxious' but is the grammar tense; the second half recalls 'practice makes perfect'.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb tense showing completed action; also flawless, the result of long rehearsal.

clue.text: Might drop in for a picture — fancy that !

indicators.note: one piece might drop into the other, so it is put inside

parts.note: an image is a picture

explanation.surface: Someone might pop in for a photo; how surprising!
explanation.walkthrough: 'drop in' looks like a casual visit, but 'drop' puts IN into IMAGE. 'Might' and 'for a' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Fancy that!' and the one-word exclamation both express surprise; to fancy is also to picture in the mind.

clue.text: Gate-crasher

parts.note: not an uninvited party guest, but a beam swung to smash city gates

explanation.definitionFit: A heavy beam used in sieges to break down gates and walls.
